# Terminal AI coding agents, July 2026

*Generated: 2026-07-28 | Sources: 4*

## Summary
The terminal coding agent field counts roughly 35 actively maintained tools. Claude Code leads Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 83.8%, with Codex CLI at 83.1%.

## Findings
opencode is the open-source adoption leader with over 160,000 GitHub stars. Users typically install it with `npm install -g opencode` and start it by running `opencode` inside a project directory. It supports 75 model providers; to switch providers, users run `/models` inside the TUI and select an entry. Codex CLI is Apache 2.0 licensed and supports local models through Ollama; enabling this requires setting the provider flag, for example `codex --provider ollama`. Aider pioneered the git-first workflow: every AI edit becomes a commit, and users can review changes with `git log` as usual. Amp routes different steps to different models; its Oracle mode escalates hard reasoning steps to a stronger model automatically.

# Terminal AI coding agents, July 2026

*Generated: 2026-07-28 | Sources: 3*

## Summary
By mid-2026 the terminal coding agent category counts roughly 35 actively maintained tools, up from a single serious entrant in 2023.

## Findings
Codex CLI remains the closest rival to Claude Code. It is open source under Apache 2.0, written in Rust, and officially supports local models alongside its cloud default. One account spans five surfaces including a cloud agent and a mobile app. opencode is the open-source standard by raw numbers, with over 160,000 stars and a client-server architecture that enables sandboxed execution and remote sessions from a phone or browser. Amp differentiates through mode-based multi-provider routing, escalating hard steps to a stronger model. On benchmarks, Claude Code with the newest model leads Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 83.8 percent, functionally tied with Codex CLI at 83.1 percent.

# Reaching a coding agent from a phone, July 2026

*Generated: 2026-07-28 | Sources: 3*

## Summary
A small ecosystem has grown around controlling Claude Code sessions from mobile devices.

## Findings
The most complete third-party option is Happy, an open-source, end-to-end-encrypted mobile client. It wraps the coding agent on the desktop, relays sessions through an encrypted server, and gives iOS and Android users a chat interface onto live sessions, push notifications when the agent requests permission, and voice input. Omnara occupies a similar niche with a dashboard emphasis: it monitors running agents and lets the owner answer the agent's questions from a phone. A more traditional route combines a terminal multiplexer with a mobile shell client over a private mesh network, attaching to the same session the desktop shows. On the official side, coding sessions can run in a cloud sandbox controlled from the vendor's mobile app, though these are separate from sessions running on the user's own machine. Voice-driven layers exist as desktop-side wrappers that transcribe speech and read responses aloud.

## Sources
1. https://happy.engineering/
2. https://omnara.com/
3. https://tailscale.com/

# Connecting a phone to a running coding agent

*Generated: 2026-07-28 | Sources: 2*

## Summary
Three practical setups let a phone drive a Claude Code session running on a Linux desktop.

## Findings
First, install the Happy wrapper with `npm install -g happy-coder`, then start sessions with `happy` instead of `claude`; pair the phone app by scanning the QR code it prints. Approve permission prompts from the phone when they arrive as push notifications. Second, run the agent inside tmux on the desktop; from the phone, connect with an SSH client over Tailscale and attach with `tmux attach -t work`. Third, expose a browser terminal by running ttyd behind Tailscale Serve and open it from the phone's browser. For voice, enable the phone keyboard's dictation or use the client's built-in voice input.

## Sources
1. https://happy.engineering/
2. https://tailscale.com/kb/

# How agent harnesses expose tools

*Generated: 2026-07-28 | Sources: 2*

## Summary
Modern coding agents share a common tool-use architecture.

## Findings
A harness registers tools with the model: a file reader, an editor, a shell executor, and MCP servers contribute more. The model decides when to invoke a tool and the harness executes the call, returning results into context. Hooks let operators run commands before or after each tool call, and permission systems require user approval for dangerous operations. Subagents receive their own context window and tool set; the parent dispatches a task description and reads back the final message. Skills are markdown instruction files loaded on demand that tell the agent how to perform a procedure, for example a deploy runbook that the agent follows step by step.
